critic_reason: Violates owner's swap-free/no interest-bearing instrument condition (requires short selling and leverage).
data_source: National central bank FX intervention bulletins (e.g., BIS, central bank websites) paired with daily EM FX spot rates.
evidence: Dominguez (1998), Journal of International Money and Finance, measured central bank intervention effects on exchange rates; this lab has not tested intervention-day follow-through in EM FX daily.
mechanism: Emerging-market central banks intervene to lean against currency moves for price stability, not profit. They are willing to lose money on intervention and have deeper pockets than speculators. Their order flow shifts the equilibrium rate for several days as the market absorbs the signal; speculators who fade intervention lose because the central bank’s objective is non-economic and persistent. The effect survives because intervention is discretionary, politically sensitive, and data arrives with a lag, limiting arbitrage.
needs_short_or_leverage: Yes: short selling and leverage (EM FX CFD).
rule: Each day, using central-bank net intervention data (USD vs the EM currency) released with a one-day lag, compute the intervention surprise as today’s intervention minus the 90-day rolling mean. If the surprise exceeds +2 standard deviations (central bank sold USD/bought EM currency), buy the EM currency/USD pair at the next day’s open; if below -2 SD (central bank bought USD/sold EM currency), sell the pair at the next day’s open. Hold exactly 5 trading days and exit at the close. No position otherwise. Sizing is fixed at one unit; no look-ahead because the intervention figure is known before the next open.
title: EM FX central bank intervention follow-through
why: Violates owner's swap-free/no interest-bearing instrument condition (requires short selling and leverage).
why_new: New mechanism (non-profit central bank order flow), new data (intervention day flags), and new market for this lab (em-fx-daily has only one prior test, none on intervention).

mechanism: The EIA Weekly Petroleum Status Report moves crude oil on the headline inventory number. Algorithmic and retail participants overreact to the surprise while ignoring offsetting details (refinery runs, imports, SPR releases). The price overshoots and reverts over the same session as liquidity providers absorb the flow. Momentum chasers lose; the effect persists because the release is scheduled, the overreaction is behavioral, and arbitrage capital is limited by the speed and risk of the initial move.
needs_short_or_leverage: Yes: short selling and leverage (energy CFD).
rule: Every Wednesday at the EIA 10:30 ET release, compute the crude inventory surprise as today’s change minus the prior 4-week average change. If the surprise is above +1.5 standard deviations of the prior 52-week surprise distribution, sell one unit of crude at 10:45 ET and buy to cover at 16:00 ET the same day. If below -1.5 SD, buy at 10:45 ET and sell at 16:00 ET. No position otherwise. The prior 4-week average is known before the release, so there is no look-ahead.
title: EIA crude oil inventory surprise same-day mean reversion
why: Violates owner's swap-free/no interest-bearing instrument condition (requires short selling and leverage).
why_new: New mechanism (headline overreaction at scheduled EIA crude release), new data (crude inventory surprise series), and energy-futures-eia has only one prior test on a different topic (natural gas storage drift).

critic_reason: Meets all rejection criteria; mechanism is economic, data available, no condition breach.
data_source: World Gold Council Gold Demand Trends (central bank purchases by month) and daily gold futures prices.
evidence: none: a new idea (central-bank gold purchase timing is not in the tested list; gold trend, autumn, overnight, and Asian-hour rules were tested, but not central-bank flow timing).
mechanism: Central banks buy gold monthly for reserve diversification and de-dollarization. They are price-insensitive, long-term buyers with no profit motive and no stop-loss. Their purchases create persistent demand that the market underreacts to because gold is usually priced through real-rate and yield lenses. Speculators fighting the flow lose; the effect persists because central bank reserve accumulation is structural, multi-year, and not arbitraged away by profit-driven traders.
needs_short_or_leverage: No short selling; no leverage required (1x gold CFD possible).
rule: At the close on the first trading day after the World Gold Council monthly Gold Demand Trends report, if net central bank gold purchases in the reported month exceed the trailing 12-month average, buy one unit of gold at the next day’s open and hold until the close on the first trading day after the next report; then reassess. If purchases do not exceed the average, remain flat. No look-ahead: the report is public before the next day’s open. One round trip per month, so spread/slippage are a small fraction of the monthly move.

mechanism: Emerging-market sovereigns and quasi-sovereign issuers must service USD-denominated debt on fixed contractual dates. Exit at the close on the fifth trading day after entry. Include only debt-service dates where the trailing 4-quarter rolling USD debt-service amount for that currency is above its own 25th percentile. Equal-weight across pairs as one book. No look-ahead: all debt-service dates and amounts are known from public calendars before the entry date.

evidence: Stivers & Sun documented expiration-week effects in US large caps; this proposal extends the structural delta-hedging mechanism globally across index CFDs as one book to answer the power critique.
mechanism: Equity index options market makers must delta-hedge into the close on expiration Friday. When aggregate open interest is concentrated at strikes away from the current index level, hedging flows push the index toward the max-pain strike. This is structural (options market-making obligations) and persists because market makers are contractually obligated to hedge and cannot opt out; the flow is mechanical, not profit-motivated. Options buyers whose strikes expire worthless due to pinning pressure are the willing losers.
needs_short_or_leverage: Yes: the rule can go short when the index close is above the max-pain strike, and uses leverage to equal-weight the index CFD book.
rule: At the close on the first trading day of the monthly options-expiration week (the week containing the third Friday), for each index CFD identify the strike with the largest combined call-plus-put open interest in the near-month expiration series, using open interest published after the prior close. If the index close is below that strike, go long the index CFD; if above, go short. Exit at the close on expiration Friday. Equal-weight across index CFDs as one book. No look-ahead: open interest is known from the prior day's publication.
title: Monthly options-expiration week index drift across global index CFDs

critic_reason: New family on an untested universe (us-treasury-daily, 0 tests) with a coherent risk-premium mechanism (inflation-risk term premium compressing as yields revert). The rule is fully causal (rolling 252-day percentile, 50-day SMA exit), H.15 yields are point-in-time and public, and Treasury CFDs exist. data_source: US Treasury daily yield data (Federal Reserve H.15) and corresponding CFD price data
evidence: none: a new idea
mechanism: Investors demand a premium for holding nominal bonds during periods of high macroeconomic uncertainty or inflation volatility. When inflation expectations spike, the required term premium increases, causing nominal bond yields to rise and bond prices to fall. Patient capital willing to bear inflation risk buys these bonds at rich yields, capturing the premium as expectations stabilize and yields revert. This persists because inflation risk is systematic and cannot be diversified away by most investors, who face constraints on holding long-duration assets during high inflation.
rule: At the daily close, compute the 10-year Treasury yield. If the current yield is in the top 10% of the rolling 252-day window, enter a long position in the 10-year Treasury CFD. Hold the position until the yield falls below its 50-day simple moving average, at which point exit to cash. If the yield is not in the top 10% at the close, remain in cash. This rule spans 2 instruments (the 10-year and 30-year Treasury CFDs) traded as one book.
title: Treasury Inflation Expectations Risk Premium

mechanism: Many emerging market currencies are heavily commodity-exporter dependent. This rule spans 4 commodity-linked EM FX currencies (BRL, ZAR, COP, MXN) traded as one book.

evidence: none: a new idea
mechanism: Information about economic conditions or sector-specific trends does not diffuse instantaneously across all sectors. Leading sectors (e.g., technology, financials, or energy) react first to macroeconomic news or earnings surprises, and lagging sectors (e.g., consumer staples, utilities, or REITs) react with a delay of several days. Institutional investors with large portfolios trade leading sectors first due to lower transaction costs or mandate constraints, while retail investors and smaller funds trade lagging sectors later, creating a persistent information diffusion drift that can be captured by buying the lagging sectors after the leaders have moved.

Hold the position for 10 trading days or exit immediately if the laggard ETF catches up and returns more than 2.0% from entry, whichever comes first. If no such pair exists, stay in cash. This rule spans 10 sector and industry ETFs traded as one book.

This version does exactly that with international sector ETFs, so it is a new test rather than a repeat. Whether a daily-rebalanced 20-position book can keep a 1.2 net Sharpe after ETF spreads is a cost and power question for the statistics, not a ground for rejection here.
data_source: Yahoo Finance daily ETF price data
evidence: none: a new idea
mechanism: When US investors rotate into or out of a sector, the resulting flows spill over to international markets due to global portfolio rebalancing and correlated trading, causing the same sector in other countries to move in the same direction with a delay. This cross-asset linkage creates a predictable lead-lag pattern.
rule: At each day's close, compute the daily return for each US sector ETF. For each international sector ETF, if the corresponding US sector ETF's return on that day is in the top half of all US sectors, go long the international sector ETF at the next open; if in the bottom half, go short. Hold for one trading day (close to close). Rebalance daily. Equal weight per position, with a maximum of 10 positions long and 10 short.

critic_reason: The volatility-managed country equity ETF family was dropped for lack of power ONLY, with the stated remedy being more years or about two independent instruments traded as one book. Thirty country ETFs over twelve years is a breadth version that answers that lack, so it is not a repeat of a closed family. The rule is a cross-sectional volatility sort rather than the dynamic scaling described in the mechanism paragraph, and the mechanism text mislabels the low-volatility/betting-against-beta effect as the volatility risk premium; the rule as written still carries a real economic mechanism (leverage constraints and lottery demand behind the low-volatility spread), and country ETF prices are obtainable outside Bloomberg. Whether a market-neutral vol-sorted country book really delivers 1.5 net is for the statistics to settle.
data_source: Bloomberg monthly ETF price data
evidence: none: a new idea
mechanism: The volatility risk premium implies that low-volatility assets earn a premium over high-volatility ones. A strategy that dynamically scales exposure to country equity ETFs based on their recent volatility can capture this premium. By applying it to a broad cross-section of countries, idiosyncratic risks are diversified.
rule: At each month-end, compute the 20-day realized volatility for each country ETF. Sort the ETFs into quintiles based on this volatility. Go long the lowest-volatility quintile and short the highest-volatility quintile, with equal weight within each quintile. Hold for one month, then rebalance. The portfolio is market-neutral and volatility-diversified.

critic_reason: The ETF NAV premium/discount family was dropped for lack of power ONLY, with the remedy stated as about nineteen years or about three independent instruments over the eight years as one book. Fifty ETFs traded as one book over eight years answers that lack, so this is a new test. Authorized-participant creation/redemption is a genuine microstructure mechanism, daily price and NAV history for a broad ETF cross-section is obtainable, and the signal is computed after the close and traded afterwards, so it can be run without look-ahead. The small size of typical premiums against the round trip, and the stale-NAV contamination for some ETF types, are matters of cost and measurement that the statistics must weigh, not grounds for rejection at this stage.
data_source: Daily ETF price and NAV data from a data vendor
evidence: none: a new idea
mechanism: ETFs often deviate from their net asset value (NAV) due to supply-demand imbalances or short-term liquidity shocks. These deviations mean revert as authorized participants create or redeem shares to arbitrage the difference. Trading a large cross-section of ETFs diversifies the idiosyncratic risks of individual ETFs.
rule: At the end of each trading day, compute the premium/discount for each ETF as (ETF price - NAV) / NAV. Rank the ETFs by this premium. Go long the quintile with the largest discounts (most negative premium) and short the quintile with the largest premiums (most positive), with equal weight. Hold for one trading day, then rebalance. Use a maximum of 10 longs and 10 shorts.

critic_reason: The COT-based commodity hedging-pressure risk premium is distinct from COT-1's FX positioning test. It has an economic risk-premium mechanism, uses public CFTC and exchange data, and the Friday-release/Monday-open timing avoids look-ahead.
data_source: CFTC Commitments of Traders weekly reports (free) and CME daily settlement prices for 20 commodity futures.
evidence: de Roon, Nijman & Veld (2000, Journal of Finance) found hedging pressure predicts futures returns; Gorton, Hayashi & Rouwenhorst (2013, Review of Finance) linked commercial positioning and commodity risk premia.
mechanism: Commercial hedgers in commodity futures pay a risk premium to speculators for bearing price risk. When commercials are unusually net short, futures are cheap and subsequently earn positive returns; when they are unusually net long, the reverse. The pressure persists because hedgers are forced to transfer risk and speculators require compensation.
